source.verification_method: All 13 pages read, including 38 references, AppendixA/Table 6 and every figure. All six figures, payoff table and key statistical tables visually inspected in rendered pages 3–4,6–7,9–10. Crossref verifies article identity/date and one bibliography correction. Raw data, code and original cited books/studies not independently fully read or reproduced.

citation.title: Anthropomorphism-based causal and responsibility attributions to robots

reading.source_scope_note: Within-person experiment with 48 young Japanese participants and three presented partner types, followed by correlational/data-selected SEM analyses. Causal versus responsibility ratings and mind attributions differ. Mind perceptions were not randomized, model selection was exploratory and statistical reporting contains unresolved conflicts.
access_limits: Entire supplied article, appendix and images read. No raw records, analysis code, preregistration, actual individual reward distribution or original 38 cited works were independently obtained.

The 2019 predecessor uses the same game design and related authors; its participants/data were not compared. It is a related source, not automatically an independent replication or verified reused dataset.
No author was contacted. Bibliographic metadata checks are not full reads of the original paper or cited books.

study.sample: 50 recruited,2 excluded because they recognized that the human partner was an experimenter, leaving 48 (24 female),ages 20–29,M23.5. Within-person randomized order of human, Sota robot and Surface computer conditions. Exclusion after detecting the deception may select for those accepting the cover story; no population/cultural causal claim follows.
study.incentives: Participants were told rewards depended on the game and given a deliberately false historical average of 500 yen. After debrief they received a fixed 1000 yen bonus above 5000 yen participation compensation regardless of outcomes, then consented again. Interpret choices as made under believed incentives, not verified final losses or actual robot financial needs.
study.game: Ten simultaneous two-choice rounds per agent; partner scripted to want-more 6 times and yield 4, shuffled independently of participant choices. Claimed face-reading AI capabilities were cover information, not the policy generating decisions. Human/robot/computer packages differ in embodiment, speech, movement and portrayal of the partner, not just isolated anthropomorphism.
study.payoffs: Both want-more:−10 each; participant wants/agent yields:+100 participant,+20 agent; participant yields/agent wants:+20 participant,+100 agent; both yield:0. This is not the standard dominant-defection prisoner’s dilemma: best response changes with partner action. Do not call every yield altruistic or infer a cooperation motive from wording alone.
study.measures: Eighteen Japanese mind-perception items before/after each condition; maximum-likelihood promax factor analysis pooled postgame ratings, mapped pre/post ratings to two factors. Morality loads with experience rather than agency here. Oblique pattern loadings over 1 are not automatically invalid correlations. Relative causal and responsibility outcomes are partner-minus-self differences of separate seven-point items, not actual causal shares, sanctions or complete accountability measures.
study.group_results: No reported omnibus agent effect for relative cause(p=.09) or relative responsibility(p=.51). Human–robot paired causal contrast reported t 47=2.94,p=.005; Bonferroni adjustment convention not fully specified. Partner-minus-self means are near−.05/−1.25/−.93 for cause and−.75/−1.31/−.78 for responsibility from rounded raw means. These do not demonstrate universal externalization of blame.
study.mind_results: Human perceived experience higher; robot perceived agency higher than human and postgame computer on reported contrasts. Mean pre/post and interaction effects are reported null, with one clearly conflicting F/p entry. Different individual-change associations can occur without a mean time effect. Invariance across agents/time and dependence in pooled factor data are not established.
study.associations: Human agency change–relative cause r−.358; robot post-agency–cause−.400 and–responsibility−.429, post-experience–responsibility+.340. Cause/responsibility correlate.754/.810/.750 across conditions. Most computer correlations are nonsignificant. The article reports FDR use but exact family/correction conventions cannot be fully reproduced from summary values.
study.SEM: Hypotheses plus observed correlations informed full models; paths removed for fit in the same 48-per-condition data. Simplified human change-agency→cause≈−.36; robot post-agency→cause≈−.40 and experience→responsibility≈+.20. Computer experience-change→responsibility is significant in full/simplified SEM despite absent correlation support. The abstract/conclusion’s broad computer-null wording must retain this distinction.
study.outcome_correlations: Table 6 has participant want-more count and both rewards, all nonsignificant. The partner’s want-more count is fixed at 6 and cannot correlate across participants under the stated protocol; the prose’s partner wording is a mistake. Null reward associations in this small restricted game do not prove money never affects attribution.
study.limits: Repeated-measures design is explicit, but omnibus dfs 2,140 and 2,276 and pooled-human/artificial t 142 are not reconciled with the stated 48-person repeated observations. Paired contrasts do account for within-person pairing. No raw rerun establishes exactly which model or row is wrong. Significant in one condition and not another is not itself a test of condition differences.

summary: Add the adaptation gap hypothesis and self-effacing bias as distinct, limited concepts. Enrich existing agency/experience, causal contribution and blame entries, preserving nulls and distinguishing own-action sense of agency. Record false benchmark/incentive constraints, statistical/model-selection limits, and verified internal/bibliographic corrections.

findings.definition: The proposal that a discrepancy between expected and experienced agent capabilities shapes the user’s impression of that agent.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary expectation–experience hypothesis; individual mind-score changes are measured, but expected versus actual capability is not independently randomized or verified.
findings.ai_proposal: Measure expectations before interaction, actual capability under a fixed task and subsequent impressions separately. Compare justified updates with expectancy-driven distortion while preserving accurate limits. For agents, avoid inflated promises or false baselines intended to shape blame; a changed assessment can be appropriate learning.
findings.novelty_rationale: A gap between expectations and experience differs from a high expectation alone, absolute capability, generic dislike or a guaranteed trust failure.

evidence.quote: inferior actual performance of an agent to prior expectation

findings.evidence_scope: Pages 3 and 11 cite original Komatsu/Yamada sources and suggest that lower-than-expected capability can worsen impressions. The game finds an individual agency-change association for the human partner, not consistent robot/computer gap effects. Original source papers are secondary here.
findings.boundary: The gap is a proposed explanatory relation, not automatically a bias or a universal failure law. User perception, verified performance and prior expectation can diverge; one changed rating or disappointing outcome does not isolate the mechanism.

findings.definition: An attribution tendency to explain failure in terms of oneself rather than external causes.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named secondary attribution-style concept; this experiment does not establish excessive self-blame or a national psychological trait.
findings.ai_proposal: Assess how success/failure explanations allocate causal credit using actual control, alternative causes and a defensible benchmark. Distinguish warranted accountability, modest presentation and unsupported self-blame. An agent should acknowledge real errors precisely rather than accept unrelated blame or infer a user’s personality from culture.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is an attribution style toward internal explanations of failure, distinct from taking responsibility for an event one did not cause (personalization) and from self-serving externalization.

evidence.quote: cause of a failure to themselves

findings.evidence_scope: The limitations section names the concept through secondary cross-cultural literature. Negative partner-minus-self mean ratings are compatible with internal attribution but do not show it is wrong, excessive or caused by culture.
findings.boundary: Appropriate accountability and justified self-correction are not bias. No comparison with real causal shares or other cultures identifies an error. Avoid treating every Japanese participant or every person accepting fault as self-effacing, clinically distressed or irrational.

findings.definition: Attributing planning, thought or intentional-action capacity to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: The mind-perception agency factor is the existing neutral attribution construct, not an additional agency-bias label.
findings.evidence_scope: Robot post-agency correlates negatively with relative causal attribution; the human association concerns within-person change. Mind perception is not randomized, and the null computer correlations do not establish a formal between-condition difference.
findings.boundary: Perceived agency, actual capability/control and one’s own sense of agency differ. The factor includes planning, thought and memory, and is not proof of sentience or moral culpability.

findings.definition: Attributing subjective feelings or sensations to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing concept while documenting the source’s different factor structure and conditional association.

evidence.quote: abilities to sense and feel emotions

findings.evidence_scope: Robot post-experience relates to relative responsibility(r.340;SEM≈.20). Human/computer correlation support is absent, while computer experience-change SEM is significant despite no matching correlation. Morality loads with experience here, so factor meaning is not assumed universal.
findings.boundary: An attribution of emotion is not actual emotion, deserved punishment or a safe design target. Cross-condition significance patterns and same-data SEM do not establish unique causal mechanisms.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility for a negative outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper explicitly separates cause from responsibility and acknowledges multiple responsibility meanings.
findings.evidence_scope: Separate partner and self responsibility items are differenced. No omnibus relative-responsibility agent effect is detected, despite mind-rating associations. The false 500 yen benchmark and fixed final bonus limit transfer to real losses.
findings.boundary: A single responsibility item is not a complete blame, sanction, duty or liability measure. Relative scores do not prove that total responsibility is conserved or that either party’s attribution is justified.

findings.definition: Retrospectively judging an agent’s causal contribution to an outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The game’s cause rating is a perceived retrospective contribution, kept separate from responsibility rather than adding another generic causal-attribution row.
findings.evidence_scope: The outcome is partner-minus-self causal rating, not an objective causal-share estimate. Overall agent contrast is nonsignificant, with a reported paired human–robot difference. Scripted partner behavior and an artificial benchmark limit inference.
findings.boundary: Actual causation, descriptive attribution and deserved blame differ. No allocation formula, fixed sum or unique counterfactual decomposition is validated by the rating.

findings.definition: Attributing successes internally and failures to external causes in a self-favoring pattern.
findings.novelty_rationale: The introduction discusses this existing concept, but mean internal-attribution patterns do not demonstrate it in the present sample.
findings.evidence_scope: Self-serving attribution is secondary background. The experiment has no success contrast or objective benchmark proving externalization; record this as a boundary note rather than a new positive effect.
findings.boundary: Neither self-blame nor external blame automatically shows a bias. Identify the actual causal role and avoid equating warranted correction with self-effacement or warranted tool criticism with blame shifting.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 6 agency pre/post main effect
source_corrections.issue: F(1,276)=14.7 is paired with p=.54 and partial eta²=.001.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The printed F and dfs imply standard p≈.000156, not.54. At least one value is wrong; a corrected F or time-effect conclusion cannot be certified without output. The discrepancy is visible in the rendered PDF, not just extraction.
Under the usual F distribution p≈.529. Both are nonsignificant, but the reported pair is numerically inconsistent. Do not invent the original correct statistic.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 4 claim rewards always below 500 yen
source_corrections.issue: The stated payoff matrix with 6 partner want-more and 4 yield actions permits 520 yen if the participant yields in all 6 first cases and wants-more in all 4 latter cases.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Below 500 may describe the realized sample, but is not guaranteed by the stated policy/payoffs. Exactly matched choices can yield 6×20+4×100=520; the full attainable distribution was not supplied.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 8 prose versus Table 6 on page 10
source_corrections.issue: Text mentions correlation with how often the partner chose want-more, but protocol fixes that count at 6 and Table 6 labels the variable as the participant’s count.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The table’s variable is participant choice count. Do not interpret it as variation in partner selfishness.

source_corrections.issue: Alicke’s Culpable control and the psychology of blame is listed in Psychological Bulletin 124.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Metadata identity only; original full article not independently read.

methodological_limits: Perceptions and attributions are measured after the same game; their associations and SEM arrow directions do not identify causal psychological pathways. Difference scores containing post values also complicate adjustment with post scores.

Small, young convenience sample, post-deception exclusions, multiple tests and same-data path selection limit stable estimates. No formal multigroup coefficient comparison or external model validation establishes different mechanisms for all agent types.

Anthropomorphic appearance, movement, speech, instructions and partner roles are bundled. Attributed feelings are not real feelings, and lower causal blame is not evidence of greater actual competence.

Overall fit improvement and near-perfect simplified indices do not prove a causal account. Full/simplified diagrams retain different variables; comparable likelihood bases and selection uncertainty are not documented.

The source explicitly recognizes that responsibility includes distinct blame, apology, punishment, compensation and accountability concepts. A single broad rating cannot settle all of them or legal liability.

Japanese nationality does not diagnose self-effacing style or individual beliefs. Internal attribution may be warranted; no objective causal benchmark establishes that participants’ self-blame is excessive.
Actual robot emotion, guilt, mind, game learning and sentient interests are not measured. Do not design emotion claims to redirect justified accountability away from responsible institutions.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The responsibility framework distinguishes causal contribution, competence, knowledge and blame. This game supports retaining those distinctions but does not validate the nine-factor DAG or convert descriptive ratings into justified liability.
Agency and experience need separate measurement and target validity; a pre/post questionnaire and a review-language proxy are different operations. Neither establishes actual mental capacities.

Performance expectations differ from an expectation–experience discrepancy. Data-selected SEM and model fit remain association evidence, as in the student survey, even when more than one analysis method is used.

deferred.reason: The existing causal-pivotality judgment captures retrospective causal contribution, while blame attribution remains separate. No generic synonym row is needed here.
Secondary interpretation, with no uncanniness scale or manipulation in this experiment.
No objective causal benchmark, success contrast or cross-cultural comparison proves a population-wide bias. Keep the named concepts without turning nationality or negative means into a diagnosis.

limitations: One article and three conditions remain one source. The 2019 paper and cited books are not credited as independently read studies. No fixed bibliography quota, new annual counts or automatic ethical edges are inferred.
